# The two invariances ISLA is built for {#sec-invariances}

**ISLA is designed around two statements about the physics that every
discretization of a boundary-driven PDE respects and most learned
surrogates do not: the answer does not depend on where the body sits in the
laboratory, and it does not depend on how the boundary was meshed.** The
first is rigid-motion equivariance, and ISLA holds it as an exact contract.
The second is discretization consistency, and ISLA holds it as a property
of the fine-mesh limit, adopted as the acceptance criterion for every
change to the architecture. This chapter defines both, says what each buys
and does not, and describes the instruments that measure them. The
mechanisms that deliver them are taught in @sec-isla. The measurements are
in @sec-robustness-density and its neighbors, and each is cited here in one
sentence.

```{python}
#| label: setup-invariances
#| include: false
import sys; sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from palette import *
import json, statistics
from pathlib import Path
RES = Path("..") / "results"
J = lambda p: json.load(open(RES / p))
mean = statistics.mean
```

## Two of the four properties are the subject of this chapter {#sec-four-properties}

**Two of the properties a discretization of a boundary-driven PDE must
have come free, and two do not.** Global interaction, the ability of every
boundary patch to influence every output, is built into every architecture
compared here, because slice routing runs over the whole boundary with no
neighborhoods or cutoffs. Units invariance comes from nondimensionalizing
the coordinates, which every model does. The two that remain, spatial
equivariance and discretization invariance, are what this chapter defines,
and they are established differently: one as a test that passes to
roundoff in float64 (@sec-isla-contracts), the other as a convergence
measurement read against a preregistered bar (@sec-principle).

## A rigid motion of the body must move the field with it {#sec-equivariance-centerpiece}

**A rigid motion of the boundary must produce the rigid motion of the
field: scalars unchanged, vectors rotated with the body.** For a steady
problem with a free-space far field and a set of global directions, the
governing equations do not know where the origin is or which way the axes
point. Only the geometry's relation to the global directions matters
(the shared-symmetry consequence of @eq-green). A surrogate that is handed
coordinates in some laboratory frame must learn that the frame is
arbitrary, from the poses the training set happens to contain. ISLA is
never handed coordinates. Positions enter only as differences to slice
anchors, the length unit is an integral of the geometry, and every scalar
the network forms is an inner product or a norm of vectors that all rotate
together (@sec-isla-frame, @sec-isla-relational). Vector outputs are
assembled in a basis that rotates with the body (@sec-isla-heads). The
result is a property of the code, not of a checkpoint. A rotated and
translated input gives the rotated output to roundoff in float64, on random
weights and a random point cloud. The test that asserts it is in the
contract table of @sec-isla-contracts. The same construction gives exact
invariance to a uniform rescaling of the geometry, because the length unit
scales with it.

### Equivariant by construction, or invariant by canonicalization {#sec-pose}

**A baseline that consumes raw coordinates can be made exactly
pose-invariant by canonicalizing its input, at about a percent of accuracy.
Against such a baseline ISLA's equivariance is not an accuracy edge, and
the book never claims one.** The two phrases mean different things. A
model is *equivariant by construction* when every operation inside it
commutes with rigid motions, so a rotated case yields the rotated
prediction to roundoff. A pipeline is *invariant by canonicalization* when
a preprocessing step estimates a frame from each case, expresses the case
in that frame, runs an ordinary model, and rotates vector outputs back. The
pipeline is invariant exactly when the frame estimate depends on the
pose-free geometry alone. The canonical frame used here sends the global
direction $\hat g_1$ to $+x$. It fixes the roll about that axis from the
area-weighted principal axes of the surface in the transverse plane, with
the sign from the third moment. Vector outputs are rotated back before
scoring.

Three things follow from measuring GeoTransolver that way on the DrivAerML
Surface task (@tbl-pose). First, GeoTransolver in the recipe frame is not
pose-robust: a random orientation multiplies its error by more than twenty.
Second, canonicalization must be in the training pipeline. Applied only at
inference to a model trained in one exact pose, it is pose-invariant but
costs 1.6 to 1.7x, because that model is hypersensitive to the sub-degree
tilt of the frame estimate. A model that sees the estimator's tilt noise
during training learns to ignore it. Third, on this data ISLA's
exact equivariance and canonicalized GeoTransolver deliver the same pose
invariance. No accuracy claim in this book is therefore attributed to
equivariance, and the pose contract is scored as a contract.

### What the contract buys, and when no canonical frame exists

**The contract is about what the model needs at inference, and it is
decisive exactly where canonicalization has nothing to work with.**
Canonicalization needs a known global direction at inference and a
principal frame whose sign can be resolved. Both hold for every vehicle,
wing and airfoil in the benchmark datasets (no DrivAerML case is within 5%
of a principal-axis degeneracy). That is why the two routes tie there.
They fail in three settings a general PDE surrogate meets:

- A problem with no distinguished global direction ($K = 0$: a body under
  a scalar load, a heat-conduction or electrostatics problem), where there
  is nothing to align $+x$ to.
- A body whose transverse inertia tensor is degenerate or whose third
  moment vanishes, where the roll or its sign cannot be fixed.
- An assembly of parts in mixed orientations, where no single frame
  canonicalizes every component.

ISLA needs neither a frame estimate nor a global direction at inference.
In these settings the contract is the difference between a working
surrogate and a model whose error a random orientation multiplies by more
than twenty (@tbl-pose). Against baselines that learn pose
from rotation augmentation rather than from a canonical frame, the contract
also earns accuracy when cases arrive in arbitrary poses. That measurement,
at the reporting protocol on the DrivAerML Surface task, is in
@sec-pose-contract.

The contract also has a clause that the aerodynamic datasets never
exercise. An output that is a *component in a frame* (a stress
$\sigma_{12}$, a displacement along a laboratory axis) is an invariant of
the body together with the frame. ISLA represents it by predicting the
tensor itself and reading the component off it (@sec-isla-heads). The
other route, supplying the dataset's axes as global vectors, is rejected:
those axes are not a datum of the PDE (@sec-pose-inputs). The clause binds
on PLAID Tensile2d, whose targets are stress components
(@sec-interior-tensile2d).

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true" title="Exact describes the algebra and the float32 path"}
The contract tests run in float64. On the trained GPU path in float32 the
contracts hold to a small residual over the validation cars. Under the
bfloat16 autocast the recipe trains with, the residual is several percent
of the prediction, most of it ordinary bfloat16 rounding. Where a contract
is load-bearing, infer in float32 (@sec-isla-contracts, @sec-using-sampler).
:::

## The answer must not depend on how the surface was meshed {#sec-discretization-centerpiece}

**The physics does not depend on how a surface was meshed, so a model's
answer must not either. The precise form of "must not" is numerical
consistency, and it is the acceptance criterion of this program.** A CFD
mesh is refined where the engineer expected gradients, so point density is
a signal about where the flow is hard. A model that reads it borrows the
mesher's judgment, a non-physical input that is absent in a new setting: a
different mesher, a different sampling law, a geometry the training set did
not contain. The rest of this part defines the criterion, draws the four
sampling draws through which it is measured, and states what "consistent"
means as a readout.

### Discretization invariance is an acceptance criterion, not a metric {#sec-principle}

**The goal of this program is an accurate surrogate reached by physically
principled means, because the principles are what carry a model to problems
it was not trained on. Accuracy can be bought later with model size, and
generalization to novel problems cannot.** The sharpest form of that rule
concerns the discretization. Under refinement of the sampling the
prediction must converge to one field, and two samplings of the same
surface must converge to the same field. A different mesher then differs
from the training mesher only by a discretization error that vanishes in
the fine-mesh limit. A falling error with more cells is not a defect. A
different answer under a different sampler at every count is.

The program therefore adopts a change to the architecture only when three
questions are answered in order. *Why* does it work, stated as a mechanism?
Is that mechanism physically principled, in the sense that a CFD
practitioner accepts it as a statement about the problem rather than about
the dataset? Does the model converge to the same field under a biased and
an area-proportional resampling as the count grows? In-distribution
accuracy alone never justifies a change. The test that decides is never a
single accuracy number. It is a convergence measurement under several
samplers at several counts, and its training-law twin, which trains a model
under two sampling laws and scores both on one independent draw. The same
requirement applies to the law a model was *trained* under: a model trained
on an area-proportional draw must score the same on the uniform draw as its
uniform-trained twin. Configurations that fail the third question are still
measured, as ablations that price the requirement. The weights-off ablation
is the standing example, and the ledger of every decision made under this
rule is @sec-principled-decisions.

### The four sampling draws {#sec-sampling-laws}

**Every discretization measurement in this book is a statement about which
cells of a surface mesh a model gets to see, and with what weight. Four
draws recur, and @fig-sampling-laws shows all four on one meshed
section.** A surface arrives as a mesh whose cells the mesher refined
where it expected gradients (leading and trailing edges here, the
A-pillars and mirrors of a car in DrivAerML). A training or evaluation
sample keeps a subset of $n$ of the $N$ cells. Each kept cell $i$ carries
its Horvitz–Thompson weight $1/\pi_i$, the reciprocal of its inclusion
probability. Any cell-weighted sum over the kept cells therefore estimates
the same surface integral without bias, whatever the draw. The four draws
differ only in $\pi_i$:

- **Uniform over cells** (the training convention of every model in this
  book): every cell kept with probability $n/N$, every weight $N/n$. The
  kept points inherit the mesher's refinement, so the model sees a point
  cloud that is dense exactly where the mesher was.
- **Stratified** (the same law, lower variance): one cell per consecutive
  run of $N/n$ cells along the Morton (Z-order) curve through the cell
  centroids, with one random offset. Same inclusion probability and
  weights as the uniform draw, but no two kept cells are neighbors and
  no run is skipped, so slice integrals have less draw-to-draw noise.
- **10:1 front/back bias** (the density-bias probe): cells with centroid
  $x$ ahead of the per-sample median draw with ten times the probability
  of the rest, kept independently (Poisson sampling) with exact $\pi_i$.
  The front of the body is over-sampled and each rear cell that is kept
  stands for about ten times more surface than a front one.
- **Area-proportional** (the law a uniform point generator over the
  *surface* produces): $\pi_i$ proportional to the cell's area, so
  the kept points are spread evenly over the surface regardless of the
  mesher's refinement. A large cell is nearly always kept and carries a
  small weight. A tiny leading-edge cell is rarely kept and carries a
  large one.

```{python}
#| label: fig-sampling-laws
#| fig-cap: >
#|   The four draws on one meshed section (a Joukowski airfoil at 6° with
#|   a mesher-like refinement at the leading and trailing edges, 400 cells;
#|   the small ticks mark the cell boundaries). Top four panels: the cells
#|   kept by each draw at an expected 80 of 400, one marker per kept cell
#|   with marker area proportional to its Horvitz–Thompson weight (how much
#|   surface it stands for). Bottom: the density of kept points along the
#|   surface for each draw, against the mesh's own cell density (gray) and
#|   the uniform-over-the-surface level (dashed). The uniform and stratified
#|   draws follow the mesh's refinement; the 10:1 bias piles points onto the
#|   front half; the area-proportional draw is flat over the surface, with
#|   the mesher's refinement moved entirely into the weights. How to read
#|   this: the draws are computed with the recipe's own inclusion rules
#|   (PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh, StratifiedSubsampleMesh); the section and
#|   its mesh are an illustration, not a dataset surface. Weights span 1 to
#|   10 under the bias and 1 to 10 under the area law here; on the
#|   DrivAerML and HiLiftAeroML meshes the area-law weights span four
#|   decades.
#| code-fold: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
N, n = 400, 80
s_fine = np.linspace(0, 1, 20001)
rho = 1 + 9 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 0.5) / 0.05) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-(s_fine / 0.035) ** 2) + 5 * np.exp(-((s_fine - 1) / 0.035) ** 2)
cdf = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(rho[1:] * np.diff(s_fine))]); cdf /= cdf[-1]
Jm = joukowski(alpha_deg=6.0, n_cells=N, frac=np.interp(np.linspace(0, 1, N + 1), cdf, s_fine))
xy, mid, w = Jm["xy"], Jm["mid"], Jm["w"]  # w = cell length, the 1-D measure
s_mid = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(w)])[:-1] + w / 2; s_mid /= w.sum()
def uniform_draw():
    return np.sort(rng.choice(N, n, replace=False)), np.full(N, n / N)
def stratified_draw():  # Morton (Z-order) systematic sample, as StratifiedSubsampleMesh
    lo = mid.min(axis=0); span = mid.max(axis=0) - lo; q = np.round((mid - lo) / span * (2**16 - 1)).astype(np.int64)
    code = np.zeros(N, dtype=np.int64)
    for b in range(16):
        for ax_ in range(2):
            code |= ((q[:, ax_] >> b) & 1) << (2 * b + ax_)
    order = np.argsort(code); step = N / n; off = rng.random() * step
    return np.sort(order[np.floor(off + step * np.arange(n)).astype(int).clip(max=N - 1)]), np.full(N, n / N)
def poisson_draw(wts):  # independent sampling with exact pi, as PoissonBiasedSubsampleMesh
    c = n / wts.sum(); pi = np.minimum(1.0, c * wts); deficit = n - pi.sum()
    if deficit > 0:
        free = pi < 1; pi[free] = np.minimum(1.0, pi[free] * (1 + deficit / pi[free].sum()))
    return np.nonzero(rng.random(N) < pi)[0], pi
x_med = np.median(mid[:, 0])
LAWS = [("uniform over cells", INK2, uniform_draw), ("stratified (Morton systematic)", VIOLET, stratified_draw),
        ("10:1 front/back bias", "#b5179e", lambda: poisson_draw(np.where(mid[:, 0] < x_med, 10.0, 1.0))),
        ("area-proportional", GREEN, lambda: poisson_draw(w.copy()))]
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(10.2, 7.4))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(3, 2, height_ratios=[0.62, 0.62, 1.0], hspace=0.35, wspace=0.04)
axes = [fig.add_subplot(gs[i // 2, i % 2]) for i in range(4)]
densities = []
for ax, (name, col, draw) in zip(axes, LAWS):
    idx, pi = draw(); ht = 1.0 / pi[idx]
    ax.plot(xy[:, 0], xy[:, 1], color=BASELINE, lw=1.0, zorder=1)
    nb = Jm["nrm"]
    for k in range(N):
        p = xy[k]; d = nb[k]
        ax.plot([p[0], p[0] + 0.05 * d[0]], [p[1], p[1] + 0.05 * d[1]], color=MUTED, lw=0.5, zorder=0)
    ax.scatter(mid[idx, 0], mid[idx, 1], s=9.0 * ht, c=col, alpha=0.85, zorder=3, lw=0)
    clean_axes(ax); ax.set_xlim(-2.3, 2.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.55, 0.62)
    ax.set_title(name, color=col, fontsize=10)
    ax.text(0.5, -0.02, f"{len(idx)} of {N} cells kept; weights 1/π from {ht.min():.1f} to {ht.max():.1f}", transform=ax.transAxes,
            fontsize=8.5, color=INK2, va="top", ha="center", path_effects=halo())
    if name.startswith("10:1"):
        ax.axvline(x_med, color=col, lw=0.8, ls=":", zorder=2); ax.text(x_med + 0.05, 0.5, "median x: 10:1 weight to the left", color=col, fontsize=8, ha="left", va="center")
    grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200); bw = 0.02
    densities.append((name, col, np.array([np.sum(np.exp(-0.5 * ((g - s_mid[idx]) / bw) ** 2)) for g in grid]) / (bw * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi)) / w.sum()))
axd = fig.add_subplot(gs[2, :]); grid = np.linspace(0, 1, 200)
mesh_dens = np.interp(grid, s_mid, 1 / (w / w.sum()) / N)
axd.fill_between(grid, 0, mesh_dens / mesh_dens.mean() * (n / w.sum()), color=GRID, zorder=0, label="the mesh itself: cells per unit length, scaled to n")
for name, col, dens in densities:
    axd.plot(grid, dens, color=col, lw=1.8, zorder=3, label=name)
axd.axhline(n / w.sum(), color=INK2, lw=0.8, ls="--", zorder=2)
axd.text(0.995, n / w.sum(), "uniform over the surface (n ÷ perimeter)", ha="right", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=INK2, transform=axd.get_yaxis_transform(), path_effects=halo())
for s_, lab in ((0.0, "trailing edge"), (0.5, "leading edge"), (1.0, "trailing edge")):
    axd.axvline(s_, color=BASELINE, lw=0.8); axd.text(s_, 1.5, lab, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=8, color=MUTED, path_effects=halo())
axd.set_xlabel("position along the surface [fraction of arclength, lower surface → leading edge → upper surface]")
axd.set_ylabel("kept points per\nunit surface length [1/chord]")
axd.set_xlim(0, 1); axd.set_ylim(0, 75); axd.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8.5)
plt.show()
```

Two of these draws also serve as *training* laws. Every model in the book
is trained under the uniform-over-cells law unless a section says
otherwise. The training-law instrument below trains each model a second
time under the area-proportional law. The measure weights are what make
the swap fair. A model that aggregates with them sees the same integrals
under all four draws. A model that averages the kept points as if they
were equally representative sees four different point clouds.

### What "consistent" means, and the instruments that read it

**A model is consistent when its prediction depends on the surface and not
on the sample, and the readout is always a ratio of the same model's error
under two draws, or the convergence of that ratio toward one as the count
grows.** Four instruments read it, and each answers a different question.

- **The inference draw.** A trained model is scored on the same validation
  cases under the uniform draw and under the 10:1 front/back bias at the
  same count, each model's input frame taken from the drawn sample (the
  *sample frame*, which is what a biased mesher delivers). The readout is
  biased ÷ uniform. A value of 1 means the prediction depends only on the
  surface. The evidence on the DrivAerML Surface task is in
  @sec-robustness-density.
- **Convergence under refinement.** The same checkpoint is scored under
  the uniform, area-proportional and biased draws at several counts, each
  error divided by the model's own uniform-draw error at the largest count.
  Consistency is a curve that approaches 1 under every sampler. A curve
  that stays flat at a different level under a different sampler is the
  defect the criterion names. The convergence measurement is in
  @sec-consistency-bench.
- **The training law.** Each model is trained twice, under the uniform and
  under the area-proportional law, and both checkpoints are scored on one
  independent uniform draw. The readout is area-trained ÷ uniform-trained.
  This is the half of the question a practitioner meets when a surrogate
  trained on one mesher's output is handed a mesh from another. The evidence
  on the HiLiftAeroML 35-wing rung and the DrivAerML Surface task is in
  @sec-training-law.
- **Where the slices sit.** Consistency of the output implies consistency
  of the internal partition. A slice whose territory on the surface keeps
  its place and outline between two draws is a function of the surface, and
  one that moves is a function of the sample. The territory probe records each
  token's dominant slice under two independent uniform draws (the
  resampling floor) and under the biased draw (the bias excess), and the
  displacement of the slice anchors between draws. The evidence is in
  @sec-territories.

**What the criterion accepts and what it does not.** Consistency is a
fine-mesh-limit property, not an exact invariance, and ISLA's construction
makes it one by design. Every slice aggregate is a measure-weighted
quadrature estimate (@sec-isla-quadrature). Under a biased draw the
estimate carries the variance of a sample whose weights span a decade, and
that variance shrinks as the count grows. A residual that falls with cell
count is therefore the expected signature of a consistent model. A
residual that stays fixed as the count grows, or a trained function that
is wrong on every draw but the one it was fitted on, is what the criterion
rejects. The book's statement of what ISLA holds is exactly this weaker,
convergent form. The exact forms it holds are the equivariance contracts
above (@sec-equivariance-centerpiece).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the mechanism is the frame as much as the aggregation"}
Two things a model reads from a sample can break consistency: the weights
it aggregates with, and the frame it expresses positions in. A plain mean
over kept points reads the mesher's refinement into every aggregate.
Measure weights fix that. A coordinate frame centered on the plain mean of
the sampled points moves when the sample density changes, and every
downstream quantity moves with it. A frame built from measure-weighted
integrals of the surface, or no frame at all, fixes that. ISLA has both
fixes (@sec-isla-quadrature, @sec-isla-frame). The ablations that add only
the first to a baseline, and that hold its frame fixed by hand, separate the
two effects and are reported with the density evidence in
@sec-robustness-density.
:::
